The Waccamaw darter (Etheostoma perlongum) attains a maximum total length of 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters] according to recent field surveys of the Waccamaw River system. Juvenile individuals grow rapidly during their first season, and field records indicate that the total length at which puberty occurs is approximately 4.9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.9 centimeters], a measurement derived from comparative assessments with the closely related species Etheostoma raneyi. The onset of gonadal activity at this modest body size reflects the darter's adaptation to its coastal plain habitat where growing seasons are warm but limited by seasonal hydrology. During the spawning period, which typically extends through the spring months, females exhibit a pattern of iteroparous reproduction that is characteristic of many small-bodied percids, depositing their adhesive eggs in clean gravel substrates within slow-moving stretches of the river.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], hatching occurs approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days] after fertilization, with the prolarvae emerging through chorionase-mediated rupture of the egg envelope. The resulting yolk-sac larvae weigh approximately 0.0009 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0009 grams] at the time of hatching, a mass that reflects the modest egg diameter of 1.2 millimeters typical for this species. These lecithotrophic larvae undergo progressive yolk absorption over the first several days post-eclosion, completing the trophic switch to exogenous feeding around the time of mouth opening. The relatively brief yolk dependence period is consistent with the darter's life history strategy of producing small, numerous offspring that can exploit warm spring temperatures to accelerate early development. Temperature plays a critical role in determining the pace of these early life stages.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for the Waccamaw darter is 5.1 grams [Wwi = 5.1 grams], an ultimate wet weight that conforms to the expected scaling relationship between body length and mass for small-bodied darter species. This relatively modest size places Etheostoma perlongum among the smaller members of its genus, though comparable to several other endemic darters of the southeastern United States. Gravid females exhibit a pronounced distension of the abdominal cavity during the spawning season, and the species' elongated, fusiform body shape is well suited to the benthic microhabitats it occupies among submerged woody debris and gravel beds in the river channel. The relationship between body size and reproductive output is constrained by the limited abdominal volume available for egg production in such a small fish.

Water temperature exerts a strong influence on the reproductive biology of this species. At an ambient temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum reproduction rate has been estimated at approximately 0.137 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 0.137 offspring per day], based on observations of spawning frequency and clutch sizes in captive breeding studies. This translates to a female producing roughly 50 offspring over the course of the breeding season, with individual clutches comprising a modest number of eggs deposited in shallow redds. The relatively low daily reproductive output compared to some other darter species may reflect the energetic constraints imposed by the Waccamaw darter's small body size and the necessity of investing in high-quality eggs with sufficient yolk reserves. Reproductive activity typically ceases when water temperatures exceed 25 °C in the late spring.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Waccamaw darter under natural conditions in the Waccamaw River system is approximately 1.5 years [am = approximately 1.5 years], based on mark-recapture studies conducted at a mean water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This relatively short life expectancy is typical of small, rapidly maturing darter species, which often exhibit high adult mortality rates due to predation pressure and seasonal environmental stressors. The species' life history is characterized by early maturation, a single or perhaps two breeding seasons per individual, and high reproductive effort concentrated in the spring months. Senescence and post-reproductive mortality occur rapidly following the spawning season, with very few individuals surviving into a second winter. The combination of rapid growth, early maturity, and short lifespan positions the Waccamaw darter firmly within the opportunistic end of the fast-slow life history continuum among freshwater fishes.
